title: The Scent of Mud
mood: Rain over the Academy, a red alert with no sender, and a name nobody gave her. Selena chose it herself.

hero.alt: Selena, a blonde student in a white school shirt and a dark choker, smiles with her eyes closed under a gray storm sky, a lollipop stick between her fingers, a gray copy of herself behind her.

segs.t: The scent of mud on that stormy night was her earliest memory of the world.
It came to her again now. Far below, the rain had turned the courtyard’s flower beds soft and black, and the smell of wet earth climbed the bell tower.
Selena sat on the tower’s roof in her uniform with her boots over the edge. A lollipop melted slowly in her cheek. Rain ran off her hair.
Silverbolt crouched beside her, blue light along its seams. It was the dragon-shaped machine she had rebuilt herself. Nobody else could make it move.
Her phone lit up on her knee. A red alert, with no sender.
In the same moment something pulled at her from inside her cells, toward the sky over the bay. It was stronger than last week.
Somebody’s pushy today,
she thought.
“Stop trying to control me.”
She said it to nobody, and swiped the alert away.
The alert went. The pull stayed, low, under everything. So did the smell of the mud. She breathed it in and let it take her back.
Terrinia, 983.
The rain woke her.
She lay in mud. When she stood, it was cold between her bare toes.
Before this there was nothing. No bed, no face. Only the rain, and now.
She wore a gown far too long for her. Its hem dragged in the mud.
The street was dark. Every window was dark. Rain hissed on the scorched ground and sent up thin smoke.
Under the roar of the downpour, people screamed. Some were close. Some were far away, and then stopped.
Others lay in the street in their nightclothes. Rain struck their faces, and they did not blink. She had no word yet for that.
In her bones something hummed. It was deep and huge, and it came from above.
She turned toward it before she saw anything. Out over the water, above the roofs, the hum had a shape: a black cloud with violet light in its belly, and something vast inside.
The hum felt like home, long before she knew the word.
She stood in the rain and listened. No tears came. Her feet stayed where they were.
Then a light came down the street.
It swung as it came, and something on it squeaked. Inside the glass a small flame leaned with each swing. Every other light in the street had died. This one had not.
A woman carried it. She was soaked to the skin, and she stopped at every doorway.
“Anyone? Call out if you can hear me!”
Nobody called out.
The lamp swung closer. Its light slid over the mud, over a hand that did not move, over the hem of the gown. Then it found her.
The woman stopped. For a breath she only looked.
Then she knelt in the mud and gathered the child up.
Warmth, all at once. It pressed in everywhere, against a cold the child had not noticed until it was gone.
The woman’s coat was wet through. Under it she was warm, and breathing hard from running. She smelled of smoke. The hot glass of the lamp hung near the child’s cheek.
The child’s face did not change.
But her arms went around the woman’s neck by themselves, and held on.
The neck felt thin under them. Easy to break. She held it anyway, and did not squeeze. She did not know why.

Later the woman brought her under a tarp lashed between two broken walls. Rain drummed on it. The living lay beneath it in a row. The woman had to loosen the child’s arms to set her down at the end of the row.
The child curled up on the wet ground, alone.
The woman picked up her lamp and went back for more. Her boots sucked at the mud, going away. The child watched the flame, doorway by doorway, until the street swallowed it.

Years later she found words for that night, and she still asked them: Why were these carbon-based lifeforms so warm, yet so fragile? Why did that warmth make the Ender cells in her blood cry out for conquest, while also stirring an instinctive desire to cling to it?
That first night she had no words. She knew one thing anyway. She was not one of them.
Above her the hum climbed. The black cloud rose into itself and was gone.
The hum went out of her bones. They felt very quiet.
Then, down the whole street, the lamps that had died buzzed and caught.
She watched every one of them come on.
By morning the living had been moved to a shelter, a long hall of cots and wet blankets.
A clerk sat at a table by the door with a box of cards. Ink stained his hand to the wrist.
“Name?” he asked the child.
She looked at his pen. One fist was closed in the hem of the woman’s coat, and she kept it there.
“Family? A street? Anything?”
Nothing.
He wrote on a card: girl, no name. He guessed her age and wrote that down too.
“Half the children in here haven’t said a word,” he told the woman. “It’s shock. Give it time.” He nodded at the fist. “Karina, she can’t hang on to your coat all day.”
The child watched his mouth make it.
Karina.
Karina was on the rescue team: the people who went into the ruins after a strike and carried out whoever was still alive.
A volunteer held out a cup of broth. The child kept her hands where they were. Someone put a dry blanket over her shoulders. She let it slide off.
Karina dug in her coat pocket. She always kept sweets there, for the children she carried out. She brought out a fruit drop in a twist of paper, unwrapped it, and held it out on her palm.
The child looked at it a long time. Then she took it.
It was the first thing she ever accepted. She did not bite it. She let it melt, slowly, until it was gone.
All that day, people came into the hall and searched the cots for faces. None of them stopped at hers.
“Nobody’s come for her,” the clerk said at dusk.
“Then she’s with me tonight.” Karina signed the team’s log.
For one night,
she wrote.
The next evening she signed again. One more night.
The clerk tapped the log. “You can’t keep doing that.”
Karina did not look up from the page. “You don’t put down someone you carried out.”
“That isn’t a rule.”
“It’s mine.” She pulled her coat on. “It’s duty.”
In all the years after, Karina never called it anything but duty.
The clerk had a list of names for children without one.
“Anna?”
The child turned her face away from his mouth.
“Rose?”
She looked past him at the rain on the windows.
On the walk home, under the dripping awnings, Karina tried her own. “Mara? Tess?”
The child only watched her mouth. She learned words that way, and kept every one to herself.
Nobody came to claim the child, so Karina kept her. After a week the clerk stopped asking, and Karina stopped signing the log.
Days later it rained again. The child knelt on a chair at the window of Karina’s flat and watched the water run down the glass.
Karina sat at the table with her coat across her knees, mending its torn pocket. The needle went in and out.
The child climbed down. She crossed the room and closed her fist in the coat, the way she had at the shelter.
A word had waited in her for days, unsaid. Anna and Rose had been the clerk’s. Mara and Tess had been Karina’s. Nobody had given her this one.
Mine.
“Selena,” she said.
It was the first word she had spoken. Where she found it, she never told anyone.
The needle stopped halfway through the cloth. Rain ticked on the glass.
Karina looked at her the way she had in the lamplight, for a long breath.
“Selena it is,” Karina said.
Then she smiled. The child watched how her mouth did it.
The next morning, at the same window, the child gave the smile back. Karina stopped with the kettle in her hand.
On the bell tower, the rain had thinned. The flower beds below lay black and shining.
The lollipop was half gone. Selena turned it in her cheek.
Her phone lit up again. Red, with no sender. The pull came with it from the sky over the bay, harder this time, and it did not ease.
She said nothing to it now. She swiped the alert away and went in out of the rain, Silverbolt clicking down the stairs behind her.
